area: Area V. Performance Maneuvers and Ground Reference Maneuvers
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how wind changes your path over the ground, and plan and fly a rectangular course, S-turns, and turns around a point to ACS standards.
why: Every takeoff and landing uses these skills: the traffic pattern is a rectangular course flown in wind, close to the ground. Holding a track while watching for traffic keeps you out of stall-spin and collision accidents.

prereading.what: Wind drift, constant-radius turns, rectangular course, turns around a point, S-turns, and each one's common errors.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 7, 7-1 to 7-10

prereading.what: The standard traffic pattern and how the rectangular course matches it.
prereading.label: AFH 8-1 to 8-4

prereading.what: Load factor in turns and why stall speed goes up with bank.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-34 to 5-35

warmup: You fly a perfect 30° bank circle with the wind blowing 20 knots. Will your path over the ground be a circle? Why or why not?

key_terms.def: The path the airplane actually makes over the ground.
Sideways movement over the ground caused by wind.
How far you point the nose into the wind so you track straight over the ground.
Speed over the ground. Slower headed upwind, faster headed downwind.
A turn that stays the same distance from a ground point. In wind you must change bank to do it.
Two 90° turns before a maneuver to look for traffic and hazards left, right, above and below.
Aileron and rudder used together so the ball stays centered: no slip, no skid.

chunks.title: Why we fly ground reference maneuvers

body.p: Ground reference maneuvers teach you to fly a set path over the ground, not just hold an attitude. They combine the four fundamentals (straight-and-level, turns, climbs, descents) into one skill you use from every takeoff to every landing [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

bullets: Basis for traffic patterns (and jobs like survey, photo and crop dusting) [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].
Builds division of attention: fly the airplane, hold the track, watch for traffic, keep an emergency landing spot in mind, and check engine gauges [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].
Teaches you to see and correct for wind drift [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

callout.text: Don't stare at one spot. A pilot fixed on one reference can't judge rate. Scan across several references to see if you are drifting toward or away from your track [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

check.q: Name two things you must do at the same time during a ground reference maneuver besides controlling the airplane.
check.a: Track the ground path and scan for hazards like other aircraft; also keep an emergency landing spot in mind and check the engine gauges [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

body.p: The airplane flies inside a moving air mass, like a boat in a river. A 10-knot wind from the right moves you 10 nm left every hour, whether you fly 90 or 180 knots [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
To fly a straight track, point the nose into the wind just enough to cancel the drift. That is the wind correction angle [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

Source for the table: [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. A wind 45° off the nose drifts you sideways at just over 70 percent of the wind speed [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]. You don't do this math in flight: just look at your references and adjust until the drift stops [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

bullets: Headed upwind: groundspeed is lower than airspeed [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].
Headed downwind: groundspeed is higher than airspeed [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].
The closer the wind is to your nose or tail, the more it changes groundspeed; the closer to the side, the less [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

callout.text: Crosswind changes your heading. Headwind and tailwind change your groundspeed.

check.q: You are flying straight along a road with the wind from the left. Which way do you point the nose?
check.a: Left, into the wind, just enough to stop the drift [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

body.p: In no wind, a constant bank makes a circle over the ground. In wind, the same constant bank makes a stretched path: the turn gets wider where groundspeed is high and tighter where it is low [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

The physics: at a given bank, more speed means a slower rate of turn and a bigger radius. Rate of turn = 1,091 × tan(bank) ÷ airspeed in knots. At 120 knots and 30° bank that is 5.25° per second, about 68.6 seconds for a full circle. At 240 knots it drops to 2.62° per second. Double the speed and the radius goes up four times [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].
So to hold a constant radius over the ground, match the bank to groundspeed [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]:

AFH example: 90 kt airspeed with a 10 kt tailwind (100 kt groundspeed). A 45° bank gives about an 890 ft radius; upwind you need only about 33° for the same radius. For a 2,000 ft radius the banks are about 24° downwind and 16° upwind [[24:150|AFH 7-4]].

callout.text: Always enter from the downwind side, where you need your steepest bank. If that bank is too steep, exit and move farther from the reference. Avoid banks over 45° because stall speed rises [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

check.q: Where in a turn around a point is your bank steepest, and why?
check.a: Headed downwind, because groundspeed is highest there and you need a faster rate of turn to keep the same radius [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

chunks.title: Pick the spot, the altitude, and clear the area

body.p: Ground reference maneuvers are generally flown 600 to 1,000 feet AGL [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. When choosing your altitude, think about [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]:

bullets: Lower looks faster over the ground, and drift should be easy to see from both sides.
Stay at least 500 ft above and 2,000 ft sideways from obstructions.
Lower means less time and glide distance if the engine quits.
What the test standard asks for (ACS: 600 to 1,000 ft AGL).

head: 14 CFR 91.119 minimum
Rule
rows: High enough to make an emergency landing without undue hazard to people or property
1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft horizontally
No closer than 500 ft to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure

body.p: Table source: [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]]. The AFH adds: stay well away from crowds, towns and herds of livestock [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

Good references: roads, railroad tracks, field boundaries, fence lines, canals, power lines, water tanks. Pick ones of similar size, and pick with wind, visibility, airspace, buildings and emergency landing fields in mind [[24:147|AFH 7-1]]. If no straight road exists, line up at least three references [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

callout.text: Before any maneuver: complete the checklist, make radio calls (such as on the practice area frequency), and make two 90° clearing turns looking left, right, above and below [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

Preflight: look up your airplane's stall speed at 50° bank (or the steepest bank you expect) in the POH so you know your margin. Stay at or below 45° bank and at or below maneuvering speed [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

check.q: You pick a field next to a small town at 700 ft AGL. Is that legal?
check.a: Not if any part of the maneuver takes you over the town: over a congested area you need 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]]. Even beside it, the AFH says stay well away from towns; pick a field away from the town [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

chunks.title: Rectangular course: your traffic pattern in practice

body.p: The rectangular course copies the airport traffic pattern. You keep the same distance from all four sides of a field while holding altitude and airspeed [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

head: Rectangular course
Traffic pattern
rows: ½ to ¾ mile from the boundaries [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]
Downwind about ½ to 1 mile from the runway [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]
Left unless markings show right turns [[24:165|AFH 8-1]]

body.p: Fly it step by step (wind on your tail on the downwind leg) [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]:

bullets: 1. Enter on downwind. Tailwind, highest groundspeed.
2. Downwind to base: steep bank, rolled in quickly; shallow it as the tailwind becomes a crosswind. Turn more than 90° so you are crabbed into the wind on base.
3. Base to upwind: medium bank, reduced as you turn into the headwind. Turn less than 90°.
4. Upwind to crosswind: shallow bank, rolled in slowly. Turn less than 90° and hold a crab toward the outside of the course.
5. Crosswind to downwind: medium bank, steepening as groundspeed builds. Turn more than 90°.

callout.text: Roll-in rate matters too: if the wind will push you into the course, roll in slowly; if it will push you out, roll in quickly [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

check.q: On which turn of the rectangular course do you need the steepest bank?
check.a: Downwind to base, where the tailwind gives the highest groundspeed [[24:152|AFH 7-6]]. In the pattern this is why a tailwind on base can cause an overshoot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

chunks.title: S-turns and turns around a point

body.p: S-turns: two equal half-circles on opposite sides of a straight road or line [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].

bullets: 1. Fly downwind and cross the line at 90°. Start a 180° turn right away with your steepest bank, rolled in quickly but not aggressively [[24:155|AFH 7-9]].
2. Shallow the bank as groundspeed drops. At the 90° point you are crosswind and must hold a crab [[24:155|AFH 7-9]].
3. Time the rollout so the wings are level just as you cross the line again [[24:156|AFH 7-10]].
4. With no delay, roll into the opposite turn. Now you are upwind, so start gentle and shallow, then steepen as groundspeed builds [[24:156|AFH 7-10]].

body.p: Example of the crab in a turn: with a 10° wind correction angle, the first 90° over the ground takes 100° of heading change and the last 90° takes only 80° [[24:156|AFH 7-10]].

Turns around a point: a 360° constant-radius turn around one small, easy-to-see point [[24:153|AFH 7-7]] [[24:154|AFH 7-8]]. Fly at least one full turn; two or more help you judge the wind [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

bullets: 1. Enter downwind at the radius you want. You may need to roll in quickly to the steepest bank so you don't drift wide [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].
2. Gradually shallow the bank until headed straight upwind (shallowest), then steepen again back to the entry point [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].
3. Downwind half: nose points toward the inside of the circle. Upwind half: nose points toward the outside [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].
4. Keep the point in sight. In a high-wing airplane flown from the left seat, the low wing can hide the point in a left turn; change altitude or radius if needed [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].

callout.text: ACS PA.V.B.S5: on S-turns, reverse the turn directly over the line. On turns around a point, turn in whichever direction the evaluator asks.

check.q: On S-turns, how should the bank be as you cross the line headed upwind and start the next turn?
check.a: Shallow, with a smooth gentle roll-in, because groundspeed is low there [[24:156|AFH 7-10]].

chunks.title: Fly it on the checkride: standards

body.p: The evaluator picks at least one ground reference maneuver. Same setup for each [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]:

bullets: 1. Checklist done, radio call made, two 90° clearing turns [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
2. Pick a reference and an emergency landing spot, away from people, towns and livestock [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
3. Figure out the wind. Set a steady, level altitude before you enter [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].
4. Enter on the downwind side [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].
5. Adjust bank and crab all the way around, with coordinated aileron and rudder [[24:152|AFH 7-6]].
6. Keep scanning: references, traffic, a quick look at instruments [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

head: ACS item
Standard
rows: 600 to 1,000 ft AGL (ACS PA.V.B.S3a, S3b, S3c)
Left or right pattern, 45° to the downwind leg (ACS PA.V.B.S3a)
Perpendicular to the reference line (ACS PA.V.B.S3b)
Appropriate distance from the point (ACS PA.V.B.S3c)
Directly over the reference line (ACS PA.V.B.S5)

callout.text: Your entry airspeed and power setting come from your POH and your instructor. The AFH only limits you to maneuvering speed or less [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

check.q: What are the ACS altitude and airspeed tolerances for this Task?
check.a: Altitude ±100 ft and airspeed ±10 knots (ACS PA.V.B.S7).

chunks.title: Low and turning: stalls, spins, CFIT, and coordination

body.p: You fly these maneuvers low and in steep turns. That mixes two killers: loss of control and controlled flight into terrain, both among the top four causes of fatal GA accidents. CFIT includes intentionally flying too low [[30:22|RMH 3-4]].

bullets: Load factor climbs fast above 45° to 50° bank. A level 60° bank is 2 Gs [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].
Stall speed goes up with the square root of load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. An airplane that stalls at 50 knots stalls at 100 knots at 4 Gs [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].
A sudden stall in a steep turn or with abrupt back pressure near the ground has caused many accidents [[1:132|PHAK 5-35]].

body.p: Uncoordinated flight makes it worse. If you skid (too much rudder into the turn) and pull back, a cross-control stall can roll you toward inverted and into a spin with little warning, which is deadly near the ground [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Feel it: in a skid you are pushed to the outside of the turn; in a slip you are pushed to the inside [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].

callout.text: Fix a bad position with a new entry, not a steeper bank. If the bank gets too steep, exit and re-enter farther out [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. Never use rudder to hurry the nose around: at low altitude stay reluctant to bank past 30° in the pattern and never skid to fix an overshoot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

check.q: Your nose isn't coming around fast enough on the downwind side of a turn around a point. What's the wrong fix and the right fix?
check.a: Wrong: push inside rudder (skid) and pull. Right: stay coordinated, and if more than about 45° is needed, exit and re-enter farther out [[24:151|AFH 7-5]], [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

chunks.title: Eyes outside: attention, traffic and distractions

body.p: These maneuvers make you look at the ground. That is exactly when traffic gets missed. More than a quarter (26.6 percent) of fatal accidents in 10 years happened in maneuvering flight, and the maneuver itself takes attention away from scanning for traffic [[16:12|AC 90-48E para 11.2.2.1]].

bullets: Look for other aircraft, including helicopters, and for towers and wires [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
Scan in short steps of no more than 10°, looking at each area at least 1 second [[16:12|AC 90-48E para 12]].
High wings block your view above; low wings block below. Bank now and then and look behind you [[16:13|AC 90-48E para 12.1]].
Make radio announcements, such as on the practice area frequency [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

body.p: Distraction and overload: a small problem can grab all your attention while the airplane drifts, sinks or slows. When overloaded, stop, think, slow down, and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. In this Task that means: fly the airplane first (altitude, airspeed, coordination), then clear for traffic, then fix the ground track.

callout.text: Aviate, look out, then track. A sloppy circle is a fail point; a midair or a stall is not survivable.

check.q: How should you move your eyes when scanning for traffic?
check.a: Short, regular movements of no more than 10°, pausing at least 1 second on each area [[16:12|AC 90-48E para 12]].

body.p: The AFH lists nearly the same errors for all three maneuvers [[24:153|AFH 7-7]], [[24:154|AFH 7-8]], [[24:156|AFH 7-10]]:

bullets: Not clearing the area, both before and during the maneuver.
Not setting a steady, level altitude before entry, then not holding it.
Misjudging wind direction.
Wrong wind correction angle, or poor constant-radius turns.
Slips and skids from uncoordinated aileron and rudder.
Rough, jerky control inputs.
Poor split of attention between flying and the ground references (rectangular course) and poor turn timing.

callout.text: Fixing on one point is the root of many of these. Keep your eyes moving across several references [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

check.q: Name three common errors the AFH lists for S-turns.
check.a: Any three: poor clearing, no level altitude before entry, not holding altitude, misjudging wind, poor constant-radius turns, rough controls, wrong wind correction angle, slips or skids [[24:156|AFH 7-10]].

scenario.title: Solo practice on a windy afternoon
scenario.setup: You are solo in a high-wing trainer practicing turns around a point at 700 ft AGL. The wind is about 20 knots. You picked a silo next to a farmhouse with cattle in the next field. On the downwind side the point keeps sliding under your left wing, so you add bank, push left rudder and pull to tighten the turn. The bank passes 50°. Your altitude is down 150 ft, and a Robinson helicopter calls on the practice frequency that it is 'low over the farms east of the lake'. That's your area.

questions.q: What was wrong with the reference you picked?
questions.a: It is next to a house and livestock. The AFH says the maneuver area should not cause disturbances and should be well away from settlements and herds of livestock [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. 700 ft AGL may meet 14 CFR 91.119 (500 ft from any person, vessel, vehicle or structure in sparsely populated areas), but in a steep, low turn that margin is easy to lose [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].

questions.q: Why is adding left rudder and back pressure at 50° bank dangerous here?
questions.a: Bank above 45° raises load factor and stall speed [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]], and a skid plus back pressure sets up a cross-control stall that can become a spin with little warning, deadly close to the ground [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

questions.q: What should you have done when the bank got too steep?
questions.a: Exit the maneuver and re-enter farther from the point [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. In a high-wing airplane in a left turn, also consider a bigger radius or different altitude so the point stays in view [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].

questions.q: How do you handle the helicopter call?
questions.a: Level the wings, stop the maneuver and look: helicopters are a named hazard at these altitudes [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Bank to uncover your blind spots and scan in 10° steps [[16:13|AC 90-48E para 12.1]], [[16:12|AC 90-48E para 12]]. Answer on the frequency and move to a different area if needed.

questions.q: You are 150 ft low. Which task comes first?
questions.a: Flying the airplane: fix altitude, airspeed and coordination before worrying about the circle. When overloaded, stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. 150 ft is outside the ±100 ft standard (ACS PA.V.B.S7).

skills.do: Make clearing turns and look for traffic, towers and wires before and during the maneuver.
skills.practice: Two 90° clearing turns every time, looking left, right, above and below; say 'clear' out loud [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

skills.do: Pick a suitable field, road or point, away from people and livestock, with an emergency landing spot nearby.
skills.practice: On every cross-country or local flight, point out roads, field edges and small landmarks you could use, and name a landing field [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

skills.do: Plan the entry: rectangular course 45° to downwind, S-turns perpendicular to the line, turns around a point at the right distance; all at 600 to 1,000 ft AGL (ACS PA.V.B.S3a-c).
skills.practice: Before each flight, sketch the maneuver with the forecast wind and mark where bank will be steepest and shallowest [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

skills.do: Correct for wind so your track stays square on the rectangle and the radius stays constant on S-turns and turns around a point.
skills.practice: Start by tracking over and then parallel to a straight road in a crosswind [[24:151|AFH 7-5]]. Fly two or more turns around a point to learn the wind [[24:153|AFH 7-7]].

skills.do: Reverse S-turns directly over the line; fly turns around a point in the direction the evaluator asks.
skills.practice: Practice turns around a point in both directions, especially the side where the wing hides the point [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].

skills.do: Split attention between flying, traffic and ground track while staying coordinated.
skills.practice: Glance at the ball during each turn; feel for being pushed outward (skid) or inward (slip) [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].

skills.do: Hold altitude ±100 ft and airspeed ±10 knots (ACS PA.V.B.S7).
skills.practice: Trim well before entry, use the horizon for pitch, and do quick instrument checks between ground references [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

quiz.q: What altitude range does the AFH give for ground reference maneuvers?
quiz.why: Generally 600 to 1,000 ft AGL [[24:148|AFH 7-2]], matching the ACS.

quiz.q: To keep a constant radius in a turn around a point, where is your bank steepest?
options: It stays the same all the way around
quiz.why: Groundspeed is highest headed downwind, so bank is steepest there [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

quiz.q: At 100 knots with a 20-knot direct crosswind, about how much wind correction angle cancels the drift?
quiz.why: The AFH example gives 12°; with 10 knots it is 6° [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

quiz.q: On a rectangular course, the turn from downwind to base should be:
quiz.why: High groundspeed needs a steep bank, and you turn more than 90° to crab into the wind on base [[24:152|AFH 7-6]].

quiz.q: How far from the field boundaries should you fly a rectangular course?
quiz.why: Fly ½ to ¾ mile away; flying too close forces very steep banks [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].

quiz.q: Over a congested area, 14 CFR 91.119 requires at least:
options: 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 2,000 ft horizontally
2,000 ft above the highest obstacle within 1,000 ft horizontally
quiz.why: 1,000 ft above the highest obstacle within a horizontal radius of 2,000 ft [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].

quiz.q: In a coordinated level turn at 60° bank, the load factor is:
quiz.why: A level 60° bank is 2 Gs, and stall speed rises with load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

quiz.q: During a turn the ball in the turn coordinator is to the outside of the turn, and you feel pushed outward. This is a:
options: Slip; add rudder into the turn
Skid; too much rudder into the turn
quiz.why: Ball and body pushed to the outside means a skid [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. Skidding turns near the ground can lead to a cross-control stall and spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

takeaways: Wind moves the airplane over the ground: crab into crosswinds, expect slower groundspeed upwind and faster downwind.
Constant radius in wind means changing bank: steepest downwind, shallowest upwind. Enter downwind.
The rectangular course is your traffic pattern in practice: 45° entry to downwind, ½ to ¾ mile out.
Stay 600 to 1,000 ft AGL, obey 14 CFR 91.119, and stay away from people, towns and livestock.
Bank 45° or less and stay coordinated. If it gets too steep, exit and re-enter, never skid.
Checkride: altitude ±100 ft, airspeed ±10 knots, keep clearing for traffic.
cfi_notes: Start with tracking over, then parallel to, a straight road before any turning maneuver [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].
Students fixate on the point and stop scanning for traffic and altitude. Ask them to call out traffic and altitude during the maneuver [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].
Link the rectangular course to the pattern on every flight: point out that a tailwind on base is why students overshoot final [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
High-wing trainers in left turns: the wing hides the point. Teach the fix (change radius or altitude) before the checkride [[24:154|AFH 7-8]].
Examiners often ask where the bank is steepest and why, how 91.119 applies to the chosen area, and what to do if bank exceeds 45°.
Have students look up stall speed at 50° bank in their POH as part of preflight planning [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
gaps: Entry airspeed, power setting, maneuvering speed and stall speed at bank are airplane-specific; use the POH/AFM.
AFH Ch 7 does not explain how to find the wind direction at the practice area in flight (for example from smoke, water or a nearby AWOS); the instructor should cover local methods.
Local practice-area frequencies and preferred practice areas are local information not found in these resources.
